title: The funniest sayings from around the world

entries.note: Covered in an earlier idiom episode; most likely it wishes bad luck so the opposite happens, as foreign equivalents like [[equivalent:in bocca al lupo]] suggest.
The Italian [[equivalent:break a leg]], which has its own set reply, [[see:crepi il lupo]].
The reply to [[see:in bocca al lupo]]; the hosts wonder whether the wolf chokes on the speaker or dies before it can swallow them.
The German [[equivalent:break a leg]], closer to the English than most foreign versions.
The Hungarian [[equivalent:break a leg]], close to the English version.
Said to a hunter before a hunt, hoping they catch no game or bird; the Russian [[equivalent:break a leg]], answered with [[see:go to hell]].
The traditional reply to the Russian good-luck wish [[see:neither fur nor feather]].

entries.term: costs an arm and a leg
entries.note: Means very expensive, since losing an arm and a leg is a heavy price; other languages name other body parts, like Spanish [[equivalent:costar un riñón]].

entries.term: cost the eyes in your head
entries.note: The French [[equivalent:costs an arm and a leg]], in which you lose both your eyes.
The Spanish [[equivalent:costs an arm and a leg]]; Jess thinks it the mildest price, since you have two kidneys.
Explained in an earlier episode: probably rain heavy enough to wash cats and dogs living in roofs out into the street.
A French [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]], the drops looking like dangling string; Rob's wife once said it in English.

entries.original: il pleut comme vache qui pisse
entries.note: A French [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]] recommended by Rob's wife Elodie, which Rob guessed correctly.
One of several French equivalents of [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]] from different eras.
One of several French equivalents of [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]] from different eras.
One of several French equivalents of [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]] from different eras.
One of several French equivalents of [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]] from different eras.
The Greek [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]].
The Croatian [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]]; Rob would rather take his chances with the cats.
The Cantonese [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]], which Jess likens to the French pissing cow.
The Bosnian [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]].
The Afrikaans [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]], naming the [[see:platanna]], a type of frog.
A type of frog, named in [[see:raining frogs and platannas]].
The Norwegian [[equivalent:raining cats and dogs]]; the hosts find the Norwegian versions adorable.
A Norwegian weather expression listed with [[see:raining female trolls]], which the hosts find adorable.
Said of something that will never happen; the hosts look at foreign equivalents such as [[equivalent:quand les poules auront des dents]].

entries.term: not in a month of Sundays
entries.note: Another English way of saying something will never happen, like [[equivalent:when pigs fly]].

entries.original: quand les poules auront des dents
entries.note: French for something that will never happen, like [[equivalent:when pigs fly]]; compare [[see:as rare as hen's teeth]].
Recalled because of [[see:quand les poules auront des dents]]; used in America as well as Britain.
French for never: it invokes a saint who doesn't exist or has no saint's day, so the day never comes, like [[equivalent:the 12th of never]].
English for a day that never comes, Rob's gloss of [[equivalent:à la Saint-Glinglin]].

entries.term: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain
entries.note: Russian for something that will never happen, like [[equivalent:when pigs fly]].

entries.term: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.translation: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.note: Swedish for a charmed, privileged life and succeeding without trying, like having a [[equivalent:silver spoon in your mouth]].
English for a privileged life, given as a match for [[equivalent:glida in på en räkmacka]], though the Swedish may be less derogatory.
Said of people who succeed despite failing, offered by Rob as a parallel to [[see:glida in på en räkmacka]].

entries.term: you've shat in the blue cupboard
entries.note: Swedish for making a blunder; blue cupboards were fancier because [[see:Berlin blue]] paint arrived in the 1800s. Compare [[equivalent:shit the bed]].
English for making a blunder, given as an equivalent of [[equivalent:bajsa i det blå skåpet]].
English for making a blunder, given as an equivalent of [[equivalent:bajsa i det blå skåpet]].

entries.term: taken a shit with your trousers on
entries.note: Said in an episode of the political comedy [[see:The Thick of It]] to someone who had put their foot in it.
English for making a blunder, likened to the Danish [[equivalent:træde i spinaten]].
Danish for making a blunder, like [[equivalent:put your foot in it]]; the hosts don't know why it's spinach and ask viewers.
Russian for making an avoidable mistake, which Jess likens to cartoon characters stepping on a rake and smacking themselves in the face.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the crab
entries.note: Mexican Spanish for daydreaming or being mentally far away, one of many such idioms across languages.
Polish for daydreaming, like [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]]; Rob suggests a blue almond is doubly pointless.
Colombian Spanish for daydreaming, like [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].
Colombian Spanish for daydreaming, with a double entendre on rooster testicles; like [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].
Venezuelan Spanish for daydreaming, like [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
entries.note: Czech or Slovak for daydreaming, a version of [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
entries.note: Peruvian Spanish version of [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

entries.term: have your head in the clouds
entries.note: The English equivalent of [[equivalent:thinking about the immortality of the crab]].
One of several Latvian phrases for daydreaming, similar to [[equivalent:have your head in the clouds]].
One of several Latvian phrases for daydreaming, similar to [[equivalent:have your head in the clouds]].
One of several Latvian phrases for daydreaming, similar to [[equivalent:have your head in the clouds]].

entries.term: lay back and think of England
entries.note: Letting your mind wander during sex, implying bad sex you wait to be over; it sounds very British and isn't used in America.

entries.term: the cat climbed onto the roof
entries.note: Portuguese for a doomed person or plan, from a joke about a servant told to break news of a cat's death gradually.

entries.term: end up like Zabłocki did with his soap
entries.note: Polish for trying to make a clever profit and losing money, from the tale of [[from:Zabłocki]], whose smuggled soap dissolved underwater.
In a Polish tale, a man who smuggled soap underwater and watched it dissolve, giving [[gave:end up like Zabłocki did with his soap]].
Jess's made-up English equivalent of [[equivalent:end up like Zabłocki did with his soap]], since raccoons wash food and cotton candy dissolves.

entries.term: greedy dog that drops his bone
entries.note: Rob tentatively compares the dog that drops its bone in the lake with [[see:end up like Zabłocki did with his soap]].

entries.term: not my circus, not my monkeys
entries.note: A favourite idiom of Jess's for disclaiming responsibility; Polish had it first, and Jess wonders whether English got it from Polish.
Spanish for hardly anyone being around, as at a poorly attended gig, like [[equivalent:one man and his dog]].
Rob's English rendering of [[equivalent:cuatro gatos]], meaning almost nobody.
Spanish for a [[equivalent:bookworm]].
A book lover, and also creatures such as [[see:silverfish]], [[see:book lice]], beetle larvae or termites that leave trails through old books.
The creatures usually called [[see:bookworm]]s, according to Jess.
Found in humid, unventilated, mouldy books; one of the real creatures behind the [[see:bookworm]].
In the sense of vermin, it needn't mean a wriggly worm and can mean an insect, as in [[see:bookworm]] and [[see:woodworm]].
Rob believes it isn't actually a worm, an example of the broad sense of [[see:worm]].

entries.term: better to have a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.original: más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando
entries.translation: better to have a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.note: A Spanish variation on [[equivalent:a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush]].

entries.term: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
entries.note: The English saying behind [[equivalent:más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando]].

entries.term: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
entries.note: A Spanish saying meaning [[equivalent:you snooze, you lose]].
English equivalent of [[equivalent:a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current]].
Suggested as Brazilian Portuguese but also Spanish, for being stuck with the bill or the blame; the hosts found no satisfying explanation for the duck.
Rob's English rendering of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]], which he notes makes a pun on a duck's bill.
One of several English equivalents of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]].
One of several English equivalents of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]].
One of several English equivalents of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]].
One of several English equivalents of [[equivalent:pagar el pato]].
The Spanish version of [[equivalent:lead a horse to water]], harder because you can't get a cat even as far as the water.
The English saying, which goes on to say you can't make it drink; compare [[equivalent:lead a cat to water]].

entries.term: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes
entries.note: Spanish warning that bad parenting or bad choices come back to haunt you, perhaps like [[equivalent?:you reap what you sow]].
Suggested by Jess as a possible equivalent of [[equivalent?:raise crows and they will peck out your eyes]].
Name of a crow that follows Jess on runs, after a witch in [[see:Terry Pratchett]]'s [[see:Discworld]] universe.

entries.term: flies don't enter a closed mouth
entries.note: Spanish advice to keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.
Spanish for causing a loud scene or big fuss, probably because a chicken you climbed on would make a fuss itself.
Covered in an earlier idiom episode; most likely from a verse in [[from?:Ecclesiastes]] about a bird carrying your voice, and many European languages invoke birds too.
The French [[equivalent:a little bird told me]], said while holding up the little finger; its origin is harder to work out.

entries.term: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.translation: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.note: The Russian [[equivalent:a little bird told me]], with a magpie bringing the news.

entries.term: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night
entries.note: Korean saying meaning if the birds don't tell, the mice will, akin to [[equivalent:a little bird told me]].

entries.term: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell
entries.note: A [[see:Cornish]] devil idiom about situations where authority should solve the problem.
A Celtic language related to Welsh and Breton that died out and was revived by dedicated people; called [[see:Kernow]] in Cornwall.
What the [[see:Cornish]] language is called in Cornwall, according to Rob.
Also talk of the devil; its longer form is 'speak of the devil and he will appear', and many languages have variants.

entries.term: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.original: wenn man vom Teufel spricht, ist er nicht weit
entries.translation: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.note: The German [[equivalent:speak of the devil]], basically the same as the English.

entries.term: when you speak of the wolf you see his tail
entries.original: quand on parle du loup, on en voit la queue
entries.translation: when you speak of the wolf you see his tail
entries.note: The French [[equivalent:speak of the devil]], invoking the wolf, which Rob links to an ancestral European fear of wolves.

entries.term: mention a wolf and the wolf is there
entries.note: A Lithuanian [[equivalent:speak of the devil]] submitted by a viewer, again featuring a wolf.

entries.term: between a dog and a wolf
entries.translation: between a dog and a wolf
entries.note: French for [[equivalent:twilight]], when fading light makes it hard to tell a familiar dog from an approaching wolf.
Rob glosses it as two lights; Jess corrects this to between lights, since [[see:between]] is related to two.
Related to [[same-root:two]], according to Jess, explaining [[see:twilight]] as between lights.

entries.term: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil
entries.original: más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo
entries.translation: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil
entries.note: Spanish saying that experience teaches more than talent.
Dutch for something so obvious you could feel it through wooden shoes, like [[equivalent:sticks out like a sore thumb]].

entries.term: sticks out like a sore thumb
entries.note: English for something obvious, given as a match for [[equivalent:op je klompen aanvoelen]].
Not an idiom, but Jess likens [[see:op je klompen aanvoelen]] to the princess feeling the pea through the mattress.

entries.term: all the Moomins are not in the valley
entries.note: Finnish for someone not all there, like [[equivalent:the lights are on but no one's home]], built on the [[see:Moomins]].

entries.term: the lights are on but no one's home
entries.note: English equivalent of [[equivalent:all the Moomins are not in the valley]].

entries.term: a few sandwiches short of a picnic
entries.note: English equivalent of [[equivalent:all the Moomins are not in the valley]].

entries.term: few cards short of a deck
entries.note: English equivalent of [[equivalent:all the Moomins are not in the valley]].
Characters from a Finnish children's book originally published in Swedish by a Finnish writer and illustrator, which makes [[see:all the Moomins are not in the valley]] fitting.

entries.term: lift the cat onto the table
entries.note: Finnish for raising an awkward subject everyone avoids, the [[equivalent:elephant in the room]]; almost the inverse of a [[see:dead cat]].
The awkward subject everyone avoids; addressing it is what [[equivalent:lift the cat onto the table]] means in Finnish.
A British political term for raising a big issue to distract from another, like putting a dead cat on the table; nearly the inverse of [[see:lift the cat onto the table]].

entries.term: Norwegians are born with skis on their feet
entries.original: nordmenn er født med ski på beina
entries.translation: Norsemen are born with ski on leg
entries.note: A Norwegian saying, beginning with [[see:nordmenn]], which Rob finds wonderfully typical of the culture.
Literally Norsemen or Northmen, meaning Norwegians, in [[see:nordmenn er født med ski på beina]].

entries.term: out on a trip, never sour
entries.translation: out on a trip, never sour
entries.note: Jess's favourite Norwegian saying, along the lines of [[equivalent:go outside and touch grass]].
Jess's English gloss of [[equivalent:ut på tur, aldri sur]].
Norwegian for circling a subject instead of saying what you mean, like [[equivalent:beating around the bush]].
Jess once explained to Rob that it comes from hunters beating bushes to scare birds out rather than going straight for them.
Turkish for someone who inserts themselves into every conversation and problem, unwelcome but always there, because parsley is in everything.

entries.term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
entries.note: Welsh for someone stingy with money, who avoids reaching into a pocket where a hedgehog would prick them.

entries.term: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.original: is fearr Gaeilge bhriste ná Béarla cliste
entries.translation: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.note: Encourages people to speak Irish even badly rather than English, carrying historical baggage; it rhymes in Irish but not in translation.
An Irish saying that hunger makes food taste better, meant optimistically.

entries.term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
entries.note: An Irish saying advising you to stay out of other people's business.

entries.term: one's head is a green pepper
entries.translation: one's head is a green pepper
entries.note: Japanese for someone empty-headed, since a green pepper is hollow with a few seeds rattling around.
Japanese for someone who trails around after someone else, as goldfish poop dangles behind the fish.

entries.term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
entries.original: Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare
entries.translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
entries.note: Japanese saying that nothing beats [[see:Nikko]]'s beauty, rhyming through a pun on [[see:kekkō]]; compare [[equivalent:see Naples and die]].
A Japanese city praised as unbeatably beautiful, with a famous shrine complex that is a World Heritage site.
Means splendid or magnificent, and puns on the sound of [[see:Nikko]] in [[see:Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare]].
A saying of [[see:Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]]: Naples is so beautiful you can die once you've seen it; used like the Nikko saying.
A reassuring Japanese saying meaning even experts sometimes make mistakes.
French from Quebec; one of Jess's first respondents summoned its speakers, who supplied several idioms.

entries.term: have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.original: avoir la langue dans sa poche
entries.translation: have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.note: Quebec French for someone shy or silent, less mocking than [[see:cat's got your tongue]].
A taunt at someone who can't or won't speak, which Jess finds derogatory, unlike [[see:avoir la langue dans sa poche]].
Quebec French for repeatedly nodding off to sleep.
Quebec French for preparing for something dramatic or exciting, like [[equivalent:fasten your seat belt]]; a [[see:toque]] here is a winter hat.
In [[see:attache ta tuque]] a winter hat; it can also mean a chef's hat or something shaped like one.
English equivalent of [[equivalent:attache ta tuque]], warning of something dramatic ahead.
Hungarian for a bad situation, mood or quality: a frog's backside is already near the ground, so beneath it is lower still, like [[equivalent:hit rock bottom]].
Rob's English equivalent of [[equivalent:under a frog's ass]], which Jess turns into 'frog bottom'.

entries.term: one is a dog, the other is a hound
entries.note: Hungarian for a pointless comparison, using two words that both mean dog, like [[equivalent:six of one, half a dozen of the other]].

entries.term: six of one, half a dozen of the other
entries.note: English equivalent of [[equivalent:one is a dog, the other is a hound]].
